questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Separate a machine rating from the output the building receives
questions.stem: In a memo to the planning committee, Nadia compares a district heat pump's rated efficiency with the useful heat it actually delivers into the building. Which statement correctly separates the two quantities?

options.text: Rated efficiency describes the machine at stated conditions; delivered heat is what the building receives
Rated efficiency and delivered temperature are one quantity in different units, so either gives the other
options.misconception: treats a machine rating and output temperature as one thing

options.text: Delivered temperature is always higher than rated efficiency, because heat leaves the machine
options.misconception: compares a temperature with an efficiency as if comparable

options.text: Rated efficiency can only be computed from delivered temperature, so the rating is secondary
options.misconception: reverses the dependency between rating and delivered output

questions.explanation: Efficiency is a property of the machine under stated conditions; delivered temperature is a property of the heat arriving at the building. They describe different sides of the system.
questions.hint: One describes the plant, the other the heat that arrives.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Read the heat pump energy balance from an input and output pair
questions.stem: A block of flats uses a heat pump that draws 12 kW of electricity and delivers 42 kW of heat. What does this pair of figures say about the energy balance of the installation?

options.text: That the installation has a coefficient of performance of 3.5, with the rest of the heat drawn from the air
options.misconception: ignores where the amplified heat actually comes from

options.text: That the heat pump moves 42 kW from ground, air or water into the flat while consuming 12 kW of electricity
That the installation wastes 30 kW at every moment, since the delivered heat exceeds the electricity
options.misconception: reads a heat surplus as energy destroyed

options.text: That the installation is short of capacity, since it delivers only 3.5 times the power it consumes
options.misconception: treats a performance ratio as a shortfall

questions.explanation: A heat pump uses work to move heat from a source, so delivered heat is source heat plus the work consumed. The ratio of 3.5 is the coefficient of performance, and no heat is destroyed.
questions.hint: Delivered heat equals source heat plus the work consumed.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the reversible limit of a heat pump
questions.stem: A district heat pump with a source temperature of 5 degrees Celsius delivers water at 45 degrees Celsius. What is the maximum theoretical coefficient of performance for a reversible machine between these two temperatures, using the Kelvin scale?
questions.explanation: The reversible limit is the hot temperature over the cold one in kelvin: 318.15 over 278.15 is about 1.14. Real machines work below it because losses are unavoidable.
questions.hint: Limit = hot temperature over cold one, in kelvin.

questions.topic: Total fuel utilisation with combined heat and power
questions.learningObjective: Explain what total fuel utilisation counts beyond electrical output
questions.stem: A combined heat and power unit is credited in one report at 38 per cent electrical efficiency and in another at 92 per cent total fuel utilisation. What does the second figure include that the first does not?

options.text: It includes the fuel that is not converted at all, because utilisation counts every fuel the plant takes
options.misconception: defines utilisation to include unconverted fuel

options.text: It includes the electricity that the plant draws for its own auxiliaries, which the electrical figure excludes
options.misconception: attributes the difference to parasitic electricity alone

options.text: It includes recoverable heat otherwise wasted, so the two figures measure different useful outputs
It includes losses inside the turbine, so the higher number reflects how well the boiler works
options.misconception: treats total utilisation as an adjusted boiler efficiency

questions.explanation: Electrical efficiency counts only the electricity delivered, while total fuel utilisation also credits useful heat recovered from the exhaust. They are different measures of the same fuel input.
questions.hint: One credits electricity; the other credits recovered heat.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the part of a load profile that wastes the most heat
questions.stem: A planner sketches a daily profile for a school: the boiler runs 07:00 to 08:00 for warm-up, idles 08:00 to 16:00 at a low load, and runs hard 16:00 to 19:00 for the occupied period. Which feature of this profile wastes the most heat?

options.text: The long idle period, because a boiler at a low setting loses most of its stored heat to the air
options.misconception: blames standby losses for heat the idle period needs

options.text: The warm-up hour, because the building is empty then and no heat can be usefully stored
options.misconception: treats pre-heating as inherently wasteful

options.text: The hard run from 16:00, because raising the flow temperature late in the day always costs more energy
options.misconception: assumes a late start is always the least efficient schedule

options.text: The idle load, because the plant is kept running at all times instead of being shut down and restarted once

questions.explanation: A plant kept running at part load burns fuel to hold an unused temperature, and losses accumulate over the idle window. Shutting down during empty hours removes most of that firing.
questions.hint: Long periods of low firing add up; short peaks do not.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Transmission loss and the square of current
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of cable losses across the load range
questions.stem: Outline a test to establish whether the mains cable between a substation and a new housing block is the limiting factor on the block's electric heating load.

answer.exemplar: The planner would record the heating load and the cable's voltage drop at several power levels, from the present minimum up to the proposed peak, logging both current and voltage at the substation and at the block. Repeating the sweep on several evenings separates the cable's contribution from the building's changing demand, and the resulting drop against current gives the effective resistance of the cable, which can then be compared with the drop a conductor of the same length would produce at that load.

questions.explanation: The test must sweep the load so the cable's contribution separates from building demand, and repeat, since evening loads are not steady. Drop over current gives the effective resistance.
questions.hint: Sweep the load and measure drop against current.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compute a capacity factor from rated power and annual energy

stimulus.body: The operator's bid is described in the memo as offering 4.2 MW of installed capacity for the site. The same memo records 18.6 GWh of generation across the year. The contracted capacity payment is calculated on the full 4.2 MW for every hour of the year.

questions.stem: Given the memo extract, what follows about the capacity factor implied by these figures?

options.text: The implied capacity factor is about 50.6 per cent, using nameplate capacity and the full 8760 hours
The implied capacity factor is about 50.6 per cent, using the hours during which the plant was generating
options.misconception: keeps the right number but uses the wrong denominator

options.text: No capacity factor can be derived, because a nameplate capacity says nothing about how much energy is produced
options.misconception: denies that the two figures together define a ratio

options.text: The implied capacity factor is about 22 per cent, since 18.6 GWh over the year is far below the nameplate
options.misconception: mangles the ratio into a figure with no clear basis

questions.explanation: Capacity factor is energy over nameplate power and the full year's hours: 18 600 MWh over 4.2 MW is 4 428 hours against 8 760, about 50.6 per cent.
questions.hint: Energy over nameplate power and the full length of the year.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why array output falls during a hot sunny afternoon
questions.stem: Explain to the planning committee why the output of the roof-mounted array in the housing scheme falls on hot sunny afternoons, when the demand for cooling is highest.

answer.exemplar: A photovoltaic module's output falls as its own cell temperature rises above roughly twenty-five degrees, and on a hot afternoon the module can reach seventy degrees or more while the air temperature stays moderate. Sunlight therefore produces less electricity exactly when a cooling demand peaks, so the array's contribution to offsetting that demand is smallest at the moment it is most valuable, and any storage or shifting of usage has to be planned around that pattern.

questions.explanation: Module output falls with cell temperature, and a hot sunny afternoon is when a roof array is hottest. It contributes least at the peak of cooling demand, so plans must allow for the mismatch.
questions.hint: Cell temperature, not air temperature, drives the loss.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a lower flow temperature improves boiler efficiency
questions.stem: A planner's memo states that a district boiler runs at 88 per cent seasonal efficiency while the same site would reach 95 per cent if the flow temperature were lowered by ten degrees. What does the comparison show?

options.text: That the flow temperature is irrelevant to efficiency, because 88 and 95 per cent are both reasonable figures
options.misconception: treats two plausible numbers as proof the cause is moot

options.text: That lower flow temperature leaves less difference to work against, so less fuel energy is lost up the flue
That the site should change fuel type, because the flue loss is the only thing a boiler cannot improve on
options.misconception: singles out fuel type as the only available lever

options.text: That the difference is measurement noise, since a seven point spread in efficiency is within normal scatter
options.misconception: dismisses a large efficiency difference as scatter

questions.explanation: Boiler losses grow with the temperature difference the heat must cross, so a lower flow temperature reduces the energy leaving with the flue gases. The comparison identifies a real lever.
questions.hint: Think about the temperature difference the boiler crosses.

questions.learningObjective: Compare a heat pump and a boiler on the energy actually bought
questions.stem: A retrofitted block has a heat pump drawing 9 kW and delivering 30 kW of heat, while the oil boiler it replaced delivered 30 kW while consuming 36 kW of fuel. What does the memo's table show?

options.text: That the heat pump saves 27 kW of fuel energy, since 36 minus 9 equals the heat delivered
options.misconception: subtracts electricity as if it were the delivered heat

options.text: That the heat pump is worse than the boiler, because a coefficient of performance of 3.3 sits below one
options.misconception: compares a performance coefficient with a boiler efficiency

options.text: The heat pump needs 9 kW of electricity to move 21 kW of heat, and that 21 kW comes from the outdoor air
That the two systems deliver the same useful heat at the same running cost, so the replacement saved nothing
options.misconception: ignores that the boiler burned fuel and the pump does not

questions.explanation: The boiler converted 36 kW of fuel into 30 kW of heat, while the pump delivers the same 30 kW from 9 kW of electricity plus 21 kW of ambient heat. Only the electricity is bought.
questions.hint: Subtract electricity from delivered heat to find heat moved.

questions.stem: One report lists electrical output at 34 per cent and heat output at 55 per cent of fuel input for a combined heat and power plant. What does that pair of percentages support, and what does it not?

options.text: That the plant delivers 89 per cent overall, and the remaining eleven per cent is the only loss
options.misconception: adds efficiencies as if the losses were one fixed remainder

options.text: That the plant is worse than a separate boiler and turbine, because splitting the percentages lowers any total
options.misconception: invents a comparison not supported by the figures

options.text: That the plant's heat output is negligible next to its electricity, since 55 per cent is barely half of 34
options.misconception: compares magnitudes of two different outputs

options.text: That 89 per cent of the fuel becomes useful output; the rest covers losses and unburnt fuel

questions.explanation: Adding the two useful outputs gives a total fuel utilisation of 89 per cent, and the rest is the plant's own losses plus what leaves unburnt. The figures describe this plant alone.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the measure that reveals the unavoidable part of a load profile
questions.stem: A planner draws the demand curve for a hospital: a flat base of medical loads, two sharp peaks at shift changes, and an overnight plateau. Which measure would show how much of the baseload is actually unavoidable?

options.text: The minimum demand held across twenty-four hours, the part of the load no shifting can remove
The peak demand, since the peaks set the capacity that must be installed
options.misconception: confuses installed capacity with unavoidable baseload

options.text: The average demand across the day, since averaging removes the influence of any single peak
options.misconception: assumes the average identifies the irreducible part

options.text: The demand during the shift-change peaks, since they are the periods of greatest clinical risk
options.misconception: reads clinical importance as physical unavoidability

questions.explanation: Load shifting moves consumption in time but cannot remove it, so the floor under the profile is what must be met anyway. Peaks set the plant's size; the floor sets the fuel bought.
questions.hint: Look for the lowest level the profile never goes below.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Transmission loss and the square of current
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement that separates cable loss from substation loss
questions.stem: The planner must quantify how much energy is lost between a substation and a new block, and how that loss changes with load. Describe the measurement.

answer.exemplar: The planner would log the current, the voltage at the substation and the voltage at the block at a series of operating points from the quiet overnight minimum through to the design peak, recording each for long enough to average out switching events. The difference between the two voltages at each point gives the drop, and dividing that drop by the current gives the effective resistance of the cable. Repeating the sweep at several times of day, and comparing the result with the expected drop for the installed conductor, separates the cable's share of the loss from the substation's own.

questions.explanation: Voltage drop scales with current, so the load must be swept rather than sampled once, and long records are needed because switching causes transients. Drop over current gives the effective resistance.
questions.hint: Sweep the current and read the voltage drop at each point.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Derive a capacity factor from an appendix and judge the conclusion

stimulus.body: The tender requires a plant of 2.0 MW rated capacity. The contractor's appendix reports 8.76 GWh generated in the most recent year and states that the plant was disconnected for eleven days for maintenance.

questions.stem: Using the appendix figures, what does the comparison between rated capacity and delivered energy show?

options.text: That the plant met its contracted output in full, because 8.76 GWh exceeds what 2.0 MW can deliver in a year
options.misconception: assumes a total energy figure confirms a capacity obligation

options.text: That the rated capacity was rarely reached: 8.76 GWh over 2.0 MW implies a capacity factor near fifty per cent
That the plant's rating is wrong, since the delivered energy does not match two megawatts for a whole year
options.misconception: treats a low capacity factor as an error in the nameplate

options.text: That the maintenance outage explains the whole shortfall, since eleven days cannot explain a gap this size
options.misconception: claims a single outage explains a large annual gap

questions.explanation: Rated capacity times the year's length is the maximum possible energy; delivered energy over that maximum is the capacity factor. At about half, the rating was met in a minority of hours.
questions.hint: Compare delivered energy with the rating's maximum.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the compounding effect of weak light and warm cells
questions.stem: Explain what a planner should tell residents about the output of the community solar array on a bright, cold day compared with a hazy, warm one.

answer.exemplar: On a cold clear day the cells stay near their efficient operating temperature and the array delivers close to its rated power even though the sun is not especially strong. On a hazy warm day the light is weaker and the cells are hotter, so output falls for two independent reasons at once. The planner should therefore promise energy on cool clear conditions, warn residents that a warm spell reduces output, and avoid reading any single week's low total as a fault in the installation.

questions.explanation: Two effects compound: weaker light lowers available power and a warm cell lowers conversion efficiency. Warm weather usually coincides with haze, so a quiet week is not evidence of a fault.
questions.hint: Light level and cell temperature pull in opposite ways.

options.misconception: ignores a persistent auxiliary load when ranking plant

The comparison is meaningless, because seasonal efficiency figures from different makers are never comparable

questions.explanation: The two figures cover different boundaries, so both must be stated on the same boundary before comparing. The pump's electricity is a real seasonal cost that the boiler figure omits.
questions.hint: Put both figures on the same system boundary first.

questions.learningObjective: Critique a numerically correct reading built on a favourable framing
questions.stem: A report states that a combined heat and power unit has a total fuel utilisation of 86 per cent and that its electrical output alone is 31 per cent. A reader concludes that 55 per cent of the fuel goes into useful heat. What is wrong with that reasoning?

The subtraction is invalid, because electrical output must be subtracted from the fuel input before the total

options.misconception: denies the plant credit for its recovered heat

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a genuine load trough from a scheduling artefact
questions.stem: A planner sketches a school's heating profile, showing a deep trough at midday and tall peaks at opening and closing. Which observation would confirm that the midday trough is a genuine load opportunity rather than a scheduling artefact?

options.misconception: relies on an unrelated comparison to support a local claim

options.text: That the trough persists at similar depth and timing on days with different timetables and occupancy
That the boiler serving the school is newer than the one at the neighbouring school
options.misconception: invents equipment differences that do not bear on it

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Transmission loss and the square of current
questions.learningObjective: Design a demonstration of losses recovered by a new cable route
questions.stem: A proposed underground cable loop is claimed to cut losses for the new development. Describe how the planner would demonstrate it.

answer.exemplar: The planner would install current transformers and voltage recorders at both ends of the loop and operate the development at a set of representative loads, from the quiet overnight base up to the evening peak, measuring current, sending-end voltage and receiving-end voltage at each point over several days. The measured drop gives the effective resistance of the existing route, and repeating the measurement with the alternative in service, or with a calculated comparison against the new conductor, shows how much of the loss the loop would recover without relying on a single operating point.

questions.explanation: The test must span the load range because loss varies with the square of current, and repeat so switching does not look like the cable's effect. Measuring drop at each load gives the loss recovered.
questions.hint: Losses vary with current squared, so sweep the load.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how seasonal light and temperature interact in array output
questions.stem: Explain to a resident meeting why the same array can produce more electricity on a clear winter day than on a clear summer day at noon.

answer.exemplar: Photovoltaic output depends on two separate things: the light reaching the cells and the temperature of the cells themselves. On a clear winter day the daylight is weak and short but the panels stay cold, and cold cells work more efficiently, so the total can match or beat a summer day. On a clear summer noon the sun is far stronger but the panels are hot, and the efficiency loss from that heat can cancel the extra light, which is why the output curve flattens and can even fall at the hottest part of the day.

questions.explanation: Light intensity and cell temperature push output in opposite directions, and the balance changes with season. A cold clear winter day can match a summer noon once the cells' advantage is counted.
questions.hint: Weaker light but cooler cells can still win.

answer.exemplar: The planner would work with the network operator to raise the link voltage during a controlled period and log current, sending-end and receiving-end voltage at a set of loads spanning the daily range. The loss in the link is the square of the current times its resistance, so the test has to span the loads and repeat at each one to average out switching. Comparing the measured drop against the drop recorded before the change at the same currents shows how much loss the higher voltage actually removes.

questions.stem: Explain why the output quoted for the development's solar array in winter and in summer should be based on measured cell temperatures rather than on ambient air temperatures.

answer.exemplar: The loss in a photovoltaic module depends on the temperature of the cells, which commonly runs well above the ambient air, particularly in bright conditions where the array is exposed while the wind is still. A winter reading taken on a cold but sunny afternoon can therefore have cells far warmer than the air suggests, and an assessment that uses air temperature alone will overstate the output of a poorly ventilated roof and understate the output of a ventilated one. Measuring cells directly makes the comparison fair and exposes the value of mounting that improves the cooling.

questions.hint: The array is not at air temperature; it is warmer.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a spring installation can beat a summer one over a month
questions.stem: Explain to a committee why a rooftop array on a school can produce more electricity in the spring than in the summer, even though the summer days are longer and brighter.

answer.exemplar: The array's output depends on both the light falling on it and the temperature of the cells. Spring offers long days with a moderate sun and panels that stay cool, so the cells work efficiently, while summer brings stronger light but panels heated well above the air, where conversion efficiency falls sharply. When the two effects are combined the spring installation can deliver more energy over a month, even though no individual spring day beats a clear summer day.

questions.explanation: Longer, brighter summer days do not guarantee more energy once cell temperature is counted, because hot cells convert less of the light reaching them. Over a month the cooler spring array can win.

questions.stem: Explain how a planner should describe the effect of raising the water flow rate through an array of photovoltaic modules.

answer.exemplar: A higher flow rate pulls more heat from the cells, so they sit closer to the air temperature and lose less efficiency, which raises output on a hot day. The gain is not free, because the pumping energy and the cost of the flow equipment come with it, and the extra cooling also reduces the output very slightly in cold conditions where the cells were already near their best temperature. The planner should therefore present the measure as a trade against pumping energy, not as a free gain.

questions.explanation: Higher flow cools the cells and raises output, but it brings pumping energy and equipment cost with it. On cold days the same measure can slightly reduce output, so it is a trade, not a free gain.

answer.exemplar: The planner would record voltages at the substation output, at the ends of the feeders, and at the far ends of a selected group of services, together with the current in each feeder, across a range of loads from the quiet overnight base to the evening peak. The drop between the substation and the feeder ends gives the losses in the primary and secondary distribution, while the drop along each service gives the service share. Repeating the sweep over several days and reporting the two shares separately makes the split testable rather than assumed.

questions.explanation: The split is measurable only if the drop is recorded at successive points along the supply, so substation, feeders and services separate. A load sweep is needed because shares differ with current.
questions.hint: Measure the drop at several points along the supply path.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Derive a utilisation figure from an appendix and judge the reading

stimulus.body: The appendix lists a nameplate capacity of 25 MW for the proposed wind array. A second line reports 92.4 GWh generated over the year with no outages recorded. A third line notes that the array is connected to the grid at a fixed capacity charge for every hour of the year.

questions.stem: On the figures given, what does the appendix show about how fully the nameplate capacity was used?

options.text: That the array delivered its full potential, since 92.4 GWh is a large share of what 25 MW could produce
options.misconception: treats a large absolute total as proof of full use

options.text: That the array ran above its rating, because 92.4 GWh exceeds the maximum possible for a 25 MW plant
options.misconception: misjudges the maximum possible annual energy

options.text: That the nameplate corresponds to about 3 700 full-output hours, just over forty per cent of the year
That the capacity charge is the figure to use when judging output, since revenue terms drive operation
options.misconception: confuses a commercial arrangement with a physical measure

questions.explanation: Annual energy over rated power gives the full-output hours: 92 400 MWh over 25 MW is about 3 696 hours, just over forty per cent of the year. The capacity charge is a commercial term, not work done.
questions.hint: Annual energy over rated power gives the full-output hours.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how roof colour and geometry change array performance
questions.stem: Explain why an array on a flat white roof can perform differently from the same array on a dark pitched roof in the same city on the same afternoon.

answer.exemplar: The two roofs put the cells at different temperatures and give them different amounts of light. A white flat roof bounces sunlight onto the underside and around the modules, while a dark pitched roof absorbs the light and warms the air that rises past the panels. On a clear afternoon the darker roof can therefore run several degrees hotter for the same irradiance, and because module efficiency falls as cell temperature rises, the darker installation delivers less from the same sun.

questions.explanation: Roof colour and geometry change both the light reaching the panels and the heat around them, so one array on two roofs is not the same installation. Efficiency falls as cells warm.
questions.hint: Think about how much hotter the cells sit on the dark roof.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Read a seasonal coefficient of performance against a seasonal efficiency
questions.stem: A committee memo sets an electric boiler's seasonal efficiency of 95 per cent beside a heat pump's seasonal coefficient of performance of 3.1 and asks which plant to approve. What is the fairest reading?

options.text: The heat pump is three times better, since 3.1 divided by 0.95 is a larger factor than either figure alone
options.misconception: divides a performance ratio by an efficiency to rank

options.text: The electric boiler is better, because a heat pump's figure depends on the weather and cannot be trusted
options.misconception: dismisses a seasonal figure because one input varies

options.text: The two figures are directly comparable, since both express useful energy out for energy in
options.misconception: misses that the fuel consumed is not the same in both cases

options.text: The heat pump delivers about three times as much heat per unit of energy bought, on a like-for-like boundary

questions.explanation: A coefficient of performance counts ambient heat and electricity consumed, so a boiler efficiency cannot be set beside it. Per unit of energy bought, the pump delivers three times the heat.
questions.hint: Ask what each ratio includes and what was bought.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compare a heat pump and a boiler on the energy actually bought
questions.stem: A different table records a heat pump at 20 kW delivered heat and 5 kW electricity, and a gas boiler at 20 kW delivered heat and 23 kW gas. What does it support?

options.text: That the pump reaches the same delivered heat for less than a quarter of the energy the boiler used
That the boiler is more efficient, because it converts a higher proportion of its input into heat
options.misconception: compares an efficiency with a coefficient of performance

options.text: That the two systems are equivalent, because both end up delivering the same twenty kilowatts
options.misconception: treats equal output as equal performance

options.text: That the pump is unsuitable for this site, because it needs electricity that the boiler does not
options.misconception: treats a different energy input as a disqualification

questions.explanation: The pump buys five kilowatts of electricity and the boiler twenty-three of gas for the same delivered heat, so the energy purchased differs by more than a factor of four. The rest comes from the air.
questions.hint: Compare the energy bought, not the heat delivered.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a coefficient of performance from measured inputs
questions.stem: A heat pump draws 30 kW of electricity and delivers 105 kW of heat. What is its coefficient of performance?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of performance is delivered heat over work consumed: 105 over 30 gives 3.5. It exceeds one because the pump moves heat rather than generating it, and stays below the reversible limit.
questions.hint: Divide the delivered heat by the electricity consumed.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Total fuel utilisation with combined heat and power
questions.learningObjective: Reject a ranking of plants made on incomparable outputs
questions.stem: A memo compares a combined heat and power plant at 85 per cent total fuel utilisation with an electric boiler at 95 per cent and concludes that the electric boiler is the better plant. Why is that conclusion not supported?

options.text: Because the combined plant's electricity should be valued at twice the price of heat, so cost must weigh in
options.misconception: insists the correct remedy is a specific price weighting

options.text: Because the figures count different useful outputs, so they measure different things, not rival versions
Because total fuel utilisation can never exceed ninety per cent for a plant that also delivers electricity
options.misconception: invents an upper bound the definition does not contain

options.text: Because an electric boiler's efficiency is measured on a different basis, making the numbers incomparable
options.misconception: overstates the incomparability of the two measures

questions.explanation: Total fuel utilisation counts electricity and heat, while an electric boiler's efficiency counts only its electricity conversion. Each sees an output the other cannot, so ranking them is meaningless.
questions.hint: Check whether both figures count the same outputs.
